roth-ira-calculator.assumptionNote: Assumes a constant annual return and that your monthly contribution stays within IRS annual limits. Earnings are shown tax-free, which assumes a qualified withdrawal (age 59.5+, account open 5+ years). Not tax advice.
benefits: Shows the real prize of a Roth IRA: decades of tax-free growth on every dollar of earnings.

faqs.a: You contribute after-tax dollars, and qualified withdrawals - including all the growth - are completely tax-free in retirement. A traditional IRA gives you a tax deduction now but taxes withdrawals later. Roth usually wins if you expect to be in the same or a higher tax bracket in retirement.
faqs.q: Roth IRA vs traditional IRA: which is better?

faqs.a: For 2026, the limit is $7,000 per year ($8,000 if you are 50 or older). This calculator assumes your monthly contribution respects that cap - if you enter $600 a month ($7,200 a year), reduce it to stay legal.
faqs.q: What is the Roth IRA contribution limit?

faqs.a: You can withdraw your own contributions at any time without tax or penalty, because you already paid tax on them. Earnings are a different story: withdraw them before 59.5 and before the account is 5 years old, and you generally owe tax plus a 10% penalty.
faqs.q: Can I withdraw money early from a Roth IRA?

faqs.a: High earners face income limits on direct Roth contributions. The common workaround is the 'backdoor Roth': contribute to a traditional IRA (no deduction), then convert it to Roth. The rules around this are fiddly, so check current IRS guidance or a tax pro.
faqs.q: What if I earn too much to contribute directly?

faqs.a: The 5-year rule says the account must be open at least 5 years before earnings withdrawals count as qualified. Each conversion also starts its own 5-year clock. It rarely bites people who open an account early and leave it alone, but it matters for backdoor Roth conversions.
Yes, and it is usually worth doing if you expect a long career of rising income. Paying tax at today's (presumably lower) rate to get decades of tax-free growth is the core Roth advantage.
faqs.q: Should a young person choose Roth?

roth-ira-calculator.formula:
Monthly rate r = annual return / 12. Months n = years x 12.
Future value = PMT x ((1 + r)^n - 1) / r, where PMT is the monthly contribution.
Earnings = future value - total contributions.
howTo: Enter your planned monthly contribution. Remember the IRS annual limit ($7,000 in 2026, $8,000 if 50+).
Set an expected annual return - 7 to 8% is a common long-term assumption for stock-heavy portfolios.
Enter how many years you will keep contributing.
See your projected tax-free total, what you put in, and what compounding earned you.
Try a lower return to see a cautious projection, or fewer years to see the cost of starting late.
keyFacts: A Roth IRA is funded with after-tax dollars, so qualified withdrawals - including all growth - are tax-free.
Growth follows the annuity formula: FV = PMT x ((1 + r)^n - 1) / r.
The 2026 contribution limit is $7,000 per year, or $8,000 if you are 50 or older.
Qualified withdrawals generally require age 59.5 and an account open at least 5 years.
Income limits restrict direct contributions for high earners; the backdoor Roth is the usual workaround.
Unlike traditional IRAs, Roth IRAs have no required minimum distributions during your lifetime.

roth-ira-calculator.quickAnswer: A Roth IRA grows tax-free: you pay tax on contributions now, then qualified withdrawals - including all the growth - cost you nothing in tax. For example, $500 a month at 8% for 30 years grows to about $745,200, even though you only contributed $180,000. That means roughly $565,200 of tax-free earnings. The catch: annual contributions are capped ($7,000 in 2026) and earnings withdrawals must generally wait until 59.5.
roth-ira-calculator.tagline: Project decades of tax-free Roth IRA growth from your monthly contributions.
roth-ira-calculator.workedExample:
$500/month, 8% annual return, 30 years:
1. Monthly rate r = 0.08 / 12 = 0.006667. Months n = 30 x 12 = 360.
2. Growth factor: (1.006667)^360 = about 10.936.
3. Future value = 500 x (10.936 - 1) / 0.006667 = 500 x 1,490.33 = about $745,200.
4. Total contributed = 500 x 360 = $180,000.
5. Tax-free earnings = 745,200 - 180,000 = about $565,200.
